intro.caption: Lesson 5-5 — volume of rectangular prisms. The Cubeland puzzle room only opens when the crew fills its bins with the exact number of unit cubes. Three reader gates and the Main Vault stand between them and the treasure.

balloons.t: The vault wants volume—how many unit cubes pack completely inside a prism.
Blurb! I am already one cube! Do I count?
First I pack one flat bottom layer: 6 cubes long by 4 cubes wide.
Then stack 5 identical layers up! That's length × width × height.

pages.caption: Packing one layer gives length × width cubes. Stacking height layers gives V = l × w × h.

balloons.t: Count the cubes in one layer first, then multiply by how many layers tall!
Bin A is 9 blocks tall! It has to hold more than Bin B!
Height alone can fool you. Multiply all three edges to check!
Flat tiles measure area in square units. Filling a 3D box uses cubic units!
Blurb! Three dimensions multiplied means cubic!
Main Vault is 10 by 6 by 4. Side chest is 5 by 4 by 3.
Find the Main Vault's volume, then how many MORE cubes it holds!
240 cubic blocks—and I didn't even guess by height this time!

win.caption: Volume measures 3D space inside a rectangular prism: V = length × width × height, always reported in cubic units.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Count the Layers
gates.prompt: A crate is 6 cubes long, 4 cubes wide, and 5 layers tall. Pack one layer, then fill the crate.
hints: Conceptual: one flat layer is length × width cubes; stacking layers multiplies that base area by the height.
Procedural: first compute 6 × 4 for one layer, then multiply by 5 layers.

steps: Practice crate: 4 cubes long, 3 cubes wide, 5 layers tall.
worked.q: A box is 5 cubes long, 2 cubes wide, and 4 layers tall. Total cubes?

items.label: Cubes in ONE layer (6 × 4):
items.aria: number of cubes in one bottom layer

fb.msg: 10 is 6 + 4. Multiply rows by columns to count the cubes in one layer.
20 is the perimeter around the edge, not the cubes covering the bottom.

items.fbDefault: Multiply 6 cubes long by 4 cubes wide.

items.label: Total cubes in 5 layers (24 × 5):
items.aria: total unit cubes filling the crate

fb.msg: 29 is 24 + 5. Multiply by 5 layers instead of adding.
15 is 6 + 4 + 5. Volume multiplies all three edges.

items.fbDefault: Multiply 24 cubes per layer by 5 layers.

gates.pass: 24 cubes per layer, 120 cubic blocks total! The first lock clicks.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Length × Width × Height
gates.badge: Prism Comparer — V = l × w × h
gates.prompt: Find the volume of Vault A (4 × 3 × 9) and Vault B (5 × 5 × 5) to see which holds more.
hints: Conceptual: a taller prism does not always have a bigger volume—all three edges matter.
Procedural: multiply length × width × height for each vault, then compare.

steps: Practice comparison: Box X is 7 × 3 × 2 = 42 cubic units. Box Y is 4 × 4 × 3 = 48 cubic units.
Even though Box X is longer (7 > 4), Box Y has the larger volume (48 > 42).
worked.q: Find the volume of a 5 × 3 × 4 prism.

items.label: Vault A volume (4 × 3 × 9):
items.aria: volume of Vault A in cubic blocks

fb.msg: 16 is 4 + 3 + 9. Multiply the three edges together.
150 is the outside surface area, not the inside volume.

items.label: Vault B volume (5 × 5 × 5):
items.aria: volume of Vault B in cubic blocks

fb.msg: 150 is the surface area of the 6 square faces (6 × 25), not volume.
25 is just one layer (5 × 5). Multiply by the height (5) too.

options.t: Vault A, because it is 9 blocks tall
options.fb: Height alone is not enough—108 cubic blocks is less than 125.

options.t: Vault B, because 125 cubic blocks > 108 cubic blocks
They hold the exact same amount

gates.pass: 125 beats 108! Dree admits taller isn't always bigger.

gates.title: Gate 3 · Unit Check
gates.prompt: Check Dree's units and make sure we are measuring volume, not surface area.
hints: Conceptual: area covers a flat 2D surface (square units), while volume fills 3D space (cubic units).
Procedural: multiplying three lengths (blocks × blocks × blocks) always produces cubic blocks.

steps: Because three inch-edges were multiplied, the unit is cubic inches (in³), not square inches (in²).
worked.q: What is the volume (with units) of a 6 cm × 3 cm × 3 cm box?

items.q: Dree found the volume of a 7 × 2 × 4 box and wrote 56 square blocks. What is wrong?

options.fb: 7 × 2 × 4 really is 56! Look at the unit word after 56.

options.t: Volume fills 3D space, so it needs cubic blocks, not square blocks

options.fb: Rectangular prisms never divide by 2 for volume.

items.q: Which question asks for volume instead of surface area?

options.t: How much wrapping paper covers the outside of a box?
options.fb: Covering the outside faces is surface area (square units).

options.t: How many unit cubes fill the inside of a rectangular prism?
How long is the tape around the top edge?
options.fb: Distance around an edge is perimeter (length units).

gates.pass: Cubic units locked in! One final vault door left.

gates.title: Boss Gate · Fill the Vault
gates.prompt: The Main Vault is 10 × 6 × 4 blocks. A side chest is 5 × 4 × 3 blocks. Unlock the vault!
hints: Conceptual: find each prism's volume separately using V = l × w × h before comparing them.
Procedural: compute 10 × 6 × 4, compute 5 × 4 × 3, then subtract to find how many more cubic blocks the Main Vault holds.

steps: Practice: Large box 6 × 5 × 4 = 120 cubic blocks. Small box 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 cubic blocks.
worked.q: How many more cubic blocks does an 8 × 4 × 2 box hold than a 6 × 5 × 2 box?

items.label: Lock 1 · Main Vault volume (10 × 6 × 4):
items.aria: volume of Main Vault in cubic blocks

fb.msg: 248 is the outside surface area, not the inside volume.
60 is just one bottom layer (10 × 6). Multiply by 4 layers too.

items.label: Lock 2 · How many MORE cubic blocks than the 5 × 4 × 3 chest?
items.aria: how many more cubic blocks the Main Vault holds

fb.msg: 60 is the side chest's volume. Subtract 60 from 240.
300 is 240 + 60, both together. Subtract to find how many MORE.

items.q: Lock 3 · The vault keypad asks: 240 what?

options.fb: Perimeter is a 1D edge length, not 3D space.
Square blocks measure flat 2D area, not 3D volume.

gates.pass: 240 cubic blocks, 180 more than the chest, and cubic units! The vault door swings wide open.

journal.heading: Lesson 5-5 — what the vault taught us
rows: Volume of a rectangular prism = length × width × height (V = l × w × h).
Length × width counts the unit cubes in one bottom layer; multiplying by height stacks the layers.
A taller box does not always hold more—check all three dimensions before comparing.
Volume fills 3D space, so always label answers in cubic units (like u³ or cubic blocks), never square units.
journal.quote: "I am one cubic slime, and I approve this vault." — Gel
